candidates.above_next: it restructures the entire language and has infected mainstream ones, a wider reach than any single abstraction built on top of it.

also.why: typing effects reorganises computation itself, so a program's shape now shows where the world is touched.

beats.why: the convergence of the two camps is an observation about where the field drifted, not a rule telling a designer which way to go.

harms: forces I/O and state into monadic plumbing
array and in-place algorithms become messier
candidates.instead_of: effects by default, unrestricted side effects
candidates.quote: many of us were consciously making a longterm bet that principled control of effects would ultimately turn out to be important, despite the dominance of effects-by-default in mainstream languages.
candidates.statement: Control effects on principle and make them explicit, even at the cost of convenience.

strongest.why: it is a moral stance on how one should program: effects are not free, they must be controlled and declared, against the mainstream default of effects everywhere.

candidates.above_next: it is the frame that reuses across every effect, where type classes are the mechanism it happens to ride on.

also.why: one small pattern covering so many notions of computation has an economy that is itself persuasive.

beats.why: the DSEL idea is a way of using the language, powerful but downstream of the abstraction that makes effects first-class values.

harms: do-notation can hide that code is effectful
a real conceptual wall for newcomers
candidates.instead_of: a single built-in notion of computation and sequencing
candidates.quote: the big advantage is conceptual. It is much easier to think abstractly in terms of computations than concretely in terms of the details of failure and success continuations.
candidates.statement: Capture any notion of computation as an abstract value you sequence, rather than wiring each effect into the language.

strongest.why: collapsing state, exceptions, IO, parsing and more under one return/bind frame is a genuine reorganisation of how sequencing is understood.

candidates.above_next: distinctive and generative, but narrower in daily reach than the semantic ground that referential transparency names.

also.why: a small principled solution to a small problem that generalised cleanly has a quiet elegance.

beats.why: bounded quantification restates what a class constraint is; it describes the mechanism rather than urging its principled use.

harms: dynamic semantics now depends on type resolution
candidates.quote: They were originally proposed early in the design process, by Wadler and Blott ... as a ... principled solution to a relatively small problem (operator overloading for numeric operations and equality).
candidates.statement: Solve overloading with one principled general mechanism, constraints on types, rather than ad hoc special cases.

strongest.why: principled overloading as a constraint over types opened a design space whose reach no one foresaw at the start.

candidates.above_next: it is the semantic footing the abstractions stand on, but more a consequence than the surface a programmer touches each day.

also.why: it takes a position that programs should be mathematical objects one can reason about, not recipes of state change.

beats.why: succinctness without boilerplate is a benefit the language delivers, not a rule choosing one road over another.

harms: referential transparency rules out cheap mutation
candidates.instead_of: programs as sequences of state changes
candidates.quote: Because of referential transparency, Haskell programs can be viewed as executable mathematics, as equations over the category of complete partial orders. In principle, at least, the specification becomes the program.
candidates.statement: Keep the language referentially transparent so programs read as executable mathematics.

strongest.why: seeing a program as equations, where in principle the specification is the program, is a frame that stays in the head.

candidates.above_next: it shapes the visible surface, where minimal surfaces is about the shape of solutions written on it.

also.why: the pride that 'Haskell is a pretty language' shows the authors were moved by the look of the thing.

beats.why: exploiting physical layout is one elegant device serving this larger aim of a mathematical surface.

harms: infix and prefix ambiguities such as negation
the layout rule grew complex enough to need formal specification
candidates.instead_of: the syntactic tradition of other programming languages
candidates.quote: The Haskell Committee wanted expressions to look as much like mathematics as possible, and thus from day one we bought into the idea that Haskell would have infix operators.
candidates.statement: Make notation follow mathematical usage and the reader's eye.

strongest.why: that expressions should look as much like mathematics as possible is a plain aesthetic commitment, taken from day one.

candidates.above_next: it is an aspiration for how solutions should look, above a stance about the design process itself.

also.why: the pleasure of a natural form recurring problem after problem is the enthusiasm that keeps the idea alive.

beats.why: that the many ways to define functions fit together is a fact about the design, not a rule to prefer the minimal form.

harms: elegance can hide cost and space behaviour
what counts as a 'natural' form is subjective
candidates.quote: solutions that feel like minimal surfaces: simple expressions that comprise significant complexity, with forms that seem natural, recurring in problem after problem
candidates.statement: Prefer the simplest expression that carries the complexity, the form that recurs naturally across problems.

strongest.why: solutions as minimal surfaces, simple expressions holding real complexity, is a clear criterion of beauty guiding how code should be shaped.

beats.why: the Haskell 98 commitment to stability is one later application of this conservatism, narrower than the stance itself.

harms: the language broke it anyway, notably with type classes
candidates.quote: we intended the language to be quite conservative, rather than to break new ground
candidates.statement: Embody tried-and-true consensus rather than break new ground.

strongest.why: it is a stance about what a language should be, embodying consensus rather than chasing novelty.
